questions.question: Foundation Define electrolysis. What type of current is used?

points.text: Electrolysis is the process of using electricity to break down an ionic compound into its elements. A direct current (DC) is used.

questions.question: Foundation Predict the products at each electrode when molten potassium iodide is electrolysed.

points.text: Cathode: potassium (K). Anode: iodine (I₂). The K⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and gain electrons. The I⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and lose electrons.

questions.question: Higher Predict the products at each electrode when copper(II) chloride solution is electrolysed. Write the half-equations.

points.text: Cathode: copper — Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (Cu is less reactive than H). Anode: chlorine — 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (Cl⁻ is a halide ion).

questions.question: Foundation Explain why cryolite is used in the extraction of aluminium.

points.text: Cryolite is mixed with aluminium oxide to lower its melting point from over 2000°C to about 900°C. This saves energy and reduces costs.

questions.question: Higher Describe how you would electroplate a steel ring with gold. State the electrodes and electrolyte used, and write the half-equation at the cathode.

points.text: Cathode: the steel ring. Anode: a piece of gold. Electrolyte: a solution containing gold ions (e.g. gold cyanide solution). At the cathode: Au⁺ + e⁻ → Au (gold deposits onto the steel ring).

questions.question: Extended Answer 6 marks: Explain the products of the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride, including half equations. <div class="

points.text: In aqueous sodium chloride, the ions present are Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺ (from water) and OH⁻ (from water). At the cathode (negative electrode), sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead of Na⁺: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Hydrogen gas is produced. At the anode (positive electrode), Cl⁻ is a halide ion and is discharged in preference to OH⁻: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Chlorine gas is produced. The overall result is that hydrogen forms at the cathode, chlorine forms at the anode, and NaOH remains in solution. markScheme.exemplarAnswer: In aqueous sodium chloride, the ions present are Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺ (from water) and OH⁻ (from water). At the cathode (negative electrode), sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead of Na⁺: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Hydrogen gas is produced. At the anode (positive electrode), Cl⁻ is a halide ion and is discharged in preference to OH⁻: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Chlorine gas is produced. The overall result is that hydrogen forms at the cathode, chlorine forms at the anode, and NaOH remains in solution. Mark scheme: 1 mark for identifying all ions present; 1 mark for H₂ at cathode with reason (Na more reactive than H); 1 mark for correct cathode half equation; 1 mark for Cl₂ at anode with reason (halide discharged); 1 mark for correct anode half equation; 1 mark for stating NaOH remains in solution.
